query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration subcritical annealing treatment after partial cold working of a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with a lamellar fcc/B2 structure will refine interfaces and reduce dislocation entanglements, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and restoring or enhancing ductility relative to the as-cold-worked condition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type) with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure; then partially cold-rolled (e.g., ~5–10% thickness reduction).
generation.intervention: Perform a short subcritical anneal at a temperature just below the recrystallization onset (e.g., 600–700 °C) for several minutes, followed by air cooling or water quenching to freeze in the refined lamellar microstructure.
generation.conditions: Applicable to EHEAs with a dual-phase (fcc and ordered B2) lamellar morphology under room to moderate service temperatures; recommended for EHEAs subject to partial cold deformation prior to annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement of the lamellar interfaces, partial recovery of dislocation cells, and the stabilization of a refined dual-phase substructure.
generation.mechanism: During subcritical annealing, dislocations rearrange or annihilate at newly formed/subdivided interfaces. This mitigates stress concentrations while preserving or refining interfaces that confer enhanced strengthening, allowing both yield strength and ductility to increase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a purely cold-rolled baseline, yield (or ultimate tensile) strength will increase by at least 10–20%, and ductility will improve by a comparable or greater percentage, enabling a simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Partially cold-worked EHEA with reduced elongation and retained strength from prior cold deformation but without additional heat treatment.
generation.boundary: If the annealing temperature is too high or dwell time is too long, excessive recrystallization or grain growth may occur, negating strength improvements; if temperatures are too low, insufficient recovery may limit ductility gains.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of strength and ductility improvement depends on alloy composition, precise annealing temperature, and cold-working level. Additional investigations are needed to optimize these parameters for different EHEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the same EHEA composition, partially cold-roll them, then vary subcritical annealing temperatures (e.g., 580 °C, 600 °C, 620 °C) and times (1–30 min). Perform standard tensile tests at room temperature after each treatment.
measurements: Tensile flow curves (yield and ultimate tensile strengths, elongation)
Microstructure characterization (SEM/TEM) to examine lamellar spacing and dislocation structures
XRD to confirm phase stability and extent of partial recrystallization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the processed samples demonstrate a statistically significant simultaneous increase in strength (≥10%) and ductility (≥10%) compared to the cold-rolled baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: In the 2014 study on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA), a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure exhibited an attractive combination of high fracture strength (~944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6% elongation) at room temperature. Cold rolling (8% thickness reduction) raised fracture stress to 1265 MPa but shrank ductility to ~9.9%, leaving the longstanding dilemma of enhancing both strength and ductility unresolved.
decision.unsolved: Despite the promising balance of strength and ductility in as-cast EHEAs, attempts to further raise strength (e.g., cold rolling) typically reduce elongation, indicating that the simultaneous improvement of both properties remains challenging. The community lacks a unifying strategy to refine and stabilize the lamellar microstructure while promoting strain hardening and maintaining plasticity in these eutectic alloys.
decision.lever: Implement a short-duration subcritical anneal after partial cold working to induce controlled recovery and stabilize a refined dual-phase lamellar substructure.
decision.why: A carefully tuned annealing step (e.g., near the onset of recrystallization) can partially relieve dislocation structures, refine the lamellar interfaces, and reduce detrimental stress concentrations introduced by cold deformation. Prior studies show that lamellar refinement and interface strengthening can raise yield strength while a partially recovered or dynamically recrystallized structure restores ductility. This addresses the strength–ductility trade-off in eutectic high-entropy alloys for structural applications.
